reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-four home runs projected at age 23, and the exit velocity profile backs up every bit of it: 93.0 mph average exit velo with a 50.8% hard-hit rate puts him among the most dangerous contact makers in the league, and the .370 xwOBA says the counting stats aren't outrunning the underlying skill. What makes this more than a raw-power story is the 12.3% walk rate sitting beside an 18.1% strikeout rate, a combination that explains how the projection gets all the way to a .363 OBP at .908 OPS. The fielding OAA is a problem, and if Tampa eventually moves him off third base the defensive drag becomes a real number on his value. But the bat profile here is legitimate enough that it survives a position change.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power profile maxes out the Statcast ceiling: .423 xwOBA, 21.8% barrel rate, 95.2 mph average exit velocity, and yet the strikeout rate sits at 29.1%, which is the one number that keeps this from being a clean story. What makes the tension tolerable is the 16.7% walk rate, which more than compensates for the swing-and-miss; a 22.3% chase rate says he's not chasing his way into those strikeouts, he's just getting beat when he swings. If the contact rate firms up even modestly, the .598 xSLG translates into the kind of full-season line that projects to 41 home runs and a .386 OBP, a franchise-centerpiece outcome. If it doesn't, he's still a dangerous everyday player, just one who forces your lineup card to absorb a lot of zeros.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The tension in the profile is the gap between how hard he hits it and how often he misses. An .88 xwOBA and 48.2% hard-hit rate say the contact is genuinely loud when it lands, but a 34.3% chase rate and 26.8% strikeout rate are the real ceiling cap, and if the discipline doesn't tighten, the raw power never fully converts. What saves the line is the walk rate, 11.7%, which is already well above the middle of the league and keeps the .363 OBP projection credible even with the swing-and-miss. Add 29.5 ft/s sprint speed, a 96th-percentile mark, and the 38 projected steals become a separate avenue to value that doesn't depend on fixing anything. The projection's 32 home runs and .509 SLG require the chase rate to stabilize, not disappear, but if it does, this is a legitimate middle-of-the-order piece with a speed floor that makes him useful even in the years when the bat goes sideways.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile reads almost identically on both sides of the ball, which is the whole argument for what he is. As a hitter, his .411 xwOBA and .575 xSLG sit at the 98th percentile, propped up by a 16.5% barrel rate and 13.9% walk rate, with the 30.1% whiff rate the one soft spot in an otherwise elite contact profile. On the mound, a 2.73 xERA and .257 xwOBA allowed tell the same story: 98.1 mph on the fastball, a 30.4% whiff rate, and a 3.8% barrel rate against him mean hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. The projection of .282/.389/.542 with 38 home runs across 692 plate appearances is just the hitting side rendered in counting stats, and the pitching numbers suggest the arm is real enough to hold. Everything here hinges on durability, because a profile this wide requires both halves to show up, and one injury collapses the value case entirely.

reports.name: Jacob Misiorowski
reports.published_report: A 40.6 K% that sits at the literal ceiling of the Statcast era is the headline, but the xERA of 1.97 is what makes this a serious profile, not a strikeout-rate novelty act. The 2625 rpm spin on a 100.6 mph fastball explains the 38.5% whiff rate, and a barrel rate of 3.0% tells you the stuff isn't just missing bats by luck — when contact happens, it's soft. The walk rate at 6.1% is the one lever: if it creeps up as lineups get deeper looks, the xwOBA of .218 gets harder to sustain at rotation volume, but right now the projection of a 2.10 ERA over 181.8 innings reads as a true ace, not a relief arm running a hot stretch.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .472 and the barrel rate at 11.3%, which together explain how a shortstop ends up projected for 36 home runs. Abrams doesn't generate that power through elite raw contact quality, his 89.8 mph average exit velo is roughly middle of the pack, but he finds barrels at a rate that punches above the raw speed, and the .352 xwOBA says the overall offensive profile is legitimate. The chase rate at 36.7% is the thing to watch: he's swinging at enough pitches outside the zone that a pitcher adjustment or a mechanical dip could soften those power numbers fast. If the barrel-finding holds and the chase rate doesn't climb further, you're looking at a plus offensive shortstop; if pitchers consistently exploit it, the .281/.352/.526 projection line has some give in it.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The 94.3 mph average exit velocity sits at the 98th percentile, and the 15.3% barrel rate and 53.1% hard-hit rate bracket it: this is genuine, extreme contact quality from a 24-year-old shortstop. The tension is entirely in that 27.7% strikeout rate, which drags his whiff numbers into the bottom third of the league and is the one thing standing between a good season and a great one. Everyday shortstop with a genuine power-speed combination, with the swing-and-miss as the only real tax on the counting stats.

He doesn't chase, with a 23.0% chase rate putting him among the more disciplined eyes in the league, but pitchers who find the zone are getting swings and misses at an alarming clip. reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .477 and the xSLG is .718, both maxing out Statcast's percentile scale, and the projection doesn't need to stretch to get there — a .317/.427/1.050 line across 684 plate appearances is just where the contact quality points. A 18.8% barrel rate paired with a 15.4% walk rate is the combination that makes him nearly impossible to game plan against: pitchers who attack the zone get barreled, pitchers who pitch around him fill the base paths. The 27.4% chase rate is the one lever that could move this profile in either direction, though it hasn't been a problem yet because the hard contact when he does swing is so punishing that even modest expansion doesn't cost him much. At full health, the floor here is a batting title candidate who hits 48 home runs in a good year; the ceiling is an MVP conversation every October.

The .251 xBA sitting right at league average tells you he hits for average because the power profile demands respect, not because he sprays the ball around. The one thing to watch: if pitchers find a consistent way to elevate his 27.1% whiff rate, the contact floor is thin enough that the average disappears before the power does.

reports.name: Kade Anderson

Ten walks in 276 batters faced — that's the whole argument. The translation puts his K/9 at 10.0 and his BB/9 at 2.0, where the MLB average sits at 3.2, which means the control isn't a mirage of a favorable environment but something that carries into an MLB context with real separation, and a K-BB% translating to 21.9% beside a 13.5% MLB norm is the same story told twice. reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: Seventy-two walks at 18 years old, across A+ & A, is the loudest thing on this card. The .420 OBP and 96th-percentile walk rate tell the same story: Willits has a feel for the strike zone that most hitters never develop, let alone at this age in full-season ball. The 42 stolen bases across those same 383 plate appearances turn a patient, on-base profile into something with genuine impact upside, and the .202 ISO suggests real pop is already building behind the approach. The translation softens things: a 12.8% walk rate that still clears the MLB mean comfortably, but an ISO at .135 that trails it, meaning the power hasn't fully arrived and the whole profile hinges on whether that gap closes as he climbs. If it does, he's an everyday shortstop with a legitimate .420 OBP skillset; if the game catches up to his swing and the pop stalls, the walk rate still makes him useful.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics live in completely different zip codes, and that split is exactly what makes Carroll's profile interesting. His 91.7 mph average exit velocity and 48.6% hard-hit rate are legitimately loud contact, yet a 28.3% whiff rate drags the xBA down to .251 while the xSLG sits at .451 — he's hitting the ball hard when he makes contact, he's just not making it often enough. What holds the whole thing together is an 11.5% walk rate and 29.7 ft/s sprint speed that turns singles into doubles and singles into runs, which is why the projection lands at 97 runs and 24 steals on a .827 OPS across 680 plate appearances. If the whiff rate creeps higher and the walks dry up, the hard-hit tools stop papering over the swing-and-miss and you've got a guy hitting well below his .252 projection with diminishing counting stats; keep both levers where they are and he's a genuine everyday centerfielder with real multi-category upside.

reports.name: Josiah Hartshorn
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the thing to watch here. Across A+ & A this year, Josiah Hartshorn has drawn 60 walks against 76 strikeouts in 399 plate appearances, a 15 BB% that translates to 10.8% at the MLB level, comfortably above the MLB norm of 8.5%. The .396 OBP and .893 OPS look loud for a 19-year-old first baseman, and the ISO of .220 shows legitimate pull-side thump, though the MLB equivalent dims to .145, right at the MLB mean, which is the honest signal about the ceiling. This profile lives or dies on whether the plate discipline actually travels up the ladder, because if the strikeout rate climbs with better fastballs and the ISO doesn't follow, what's left is a patient hitter without enough thump for the position. Either a second-division regular who gets on base enough to carry the corner, or a bench piece whose walk rate becomes the only tool that shows.

His xERA sits at 5.06 and hitters are barreling him up at 9.6% with a 45.0% hard-hit rate, both of which paint a picture of a reliever getting hit hard when contact happens. The one genuinely encouraging piece: 2453 rpm on the fastball is elite spin, and 95.5 mph gives him something to build on, but his 24.8% whiff rate and 21.0% K% are middling for a reliever, and 11.2% walks compound the damage every time a hitter makes contact. reports.name: Nasim Nuñez
reports.published_report: Fifty-two projected steals out of a .618 OPS is not a typo — it's the whole tension. Nuñez runs at 29.7 ft/s, 97th percentile, and his 10.6% walk rate is good enough to manufacture baserunning opportunities against a league that will happily let him reach, knowing his 84.5 mph average exit velocity and 0.4% barrel rate mean he's not going to hurt you with the bat. The xSLG sits at .277, first percentile, so the gap between what the speed can do and what the bat can do is about as wide as it gets at a big-league roster spot. If he keeps getting on base, the walk rate is the load-bearing wall here, and he's a legitimate stolen-base weapon who earns his lineup spot defensively; if that walk rate erodes and pitchers start challenging him knowing the power is essentially absent, what's left is a very fast out.

reports.name: Liam Hicks

reports.name: Logan Henderson
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile looks like a mid-rotation ace and the projection looks like a swingman. That gap is the whole read on Logan Henderson.

His xERA sits at 2.69 and he's striking out 32.0% of hitters while walking only 5.3%, a command-and-contact-suppression combination that genuinely produces ace-caliber results when it holds. The problem the profile quietly flags is that his 30.7% chase rate sits right at league average, meaning hitters aren't chasing his stuff out of the zone, so the strikeouts are coming from in-zone swing-and-miss rather than deception-driven expansion, and that's a thinner foundation than it looks. If the 28.2% whiff rate stays where it is and the walks stay low, Henderson produces those ERA and WHIP numbers across whatever innings he's given; if hitters adjust to the zone and his whiff rate softens even slightly, the strikeout rate is the first thing to fall and the projection's 88.4 innings and 3.26 ERA starts to look like a ceiling rather than a floor.

Morabito's .381 OBP across 388 plate appearances shows genuine plate discipline, 49 walks, a walk rate that translates to 10.5% at the MLB level while the league sits around 8.5%, and that on-base ability is what makes the speed meaningful rather than incidental. The power translation is the problem: his .143 ISO at AAA flattens to .127 in MLB context, well below average, and without a power jump there's no path to everyday value regardless of how many bags he takes. If the contact and the walk rate hold in the majors, he's a useful bench center fielder who can get on base and run; if the strikeout rate (23.4% equivalent) creeps up against better stuff, the whole profile collapses to organizational depth.

reports.name: Eduardo Quintero
reports.published_report: The .425 OBP is the loudest thing in this profile, and the 36 stolen bases in 365 A+ plate appearances give it legs. Eduardo Quintero walks at a rate that translates to 11.6% at the MLB level, a figure that would clear most everyday lineups comfortably, so the on-base skill appears genuinely portable. The concern is everything else: his .382 BABIP is doing heavy lifting on the batting average, the ISO translates to .133 where the MLB average sits at .150, and a 20-year-old center fielder whose ceiling is framed as organizational depth isn't being misread as a hidden gem. If the hit tool and speed hold a BABIP in the high-.300s, he's a table-setter with enough instincts to stick on a roster; if that BABIP regresses and the power doesn't grow, what's left is a bench piece who runs well.

reports.name: Nestor German
reports.published_report: The walk profile is doing the heavy lifting here. At AAA in 2026, German has held a 3.2 BB/9 across 96.7 innings, and that command translates almost flat to MLB, where the equivalent line comes out to 3.3 BB/9 — essentially indistinguishable from what big-league starters are posting. The strikeouts are a different story: 9.6 K/9 at AAA becomes 8.5 on translation, right in the thick of average MLB strikeout rates, which makes the margin thin. Everything here rests on whether the command holds at the next level, because if it does he's a functional multi-inning arm or setup piece; if the walks creep up even modestly, there's nothing left to carry him past depth-arm utility.

reports.name: Charles Davalan
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power combination at A+ is loud enough to make you look twice. Charles Davalan is hitting .287/.403/.525 across 392 plate appearances at A+, with only 43 strikeouts against 49 walks, and the K% translates to an MLB-equivalent 16.5% in a league where the average hitter strikes out at a 22.0% clip. That's the rarest thing in a teenager-adjacent bat: genuine pop, a patient approach, and almost no contact cost, and the 15 stolen bases suggest he can hurt you a third way. The ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, two to three years out, and the whole profile hinges on whether the .158 MLB-equivalent ISO holds as he climbs levels, because if the power bleeds out in the upper minors, what's left is a useful bench piece rather than an everyday contributor.

reports.name: Jarren Duran
reports.published_report: The legs are the only thing keeping this profile afloat. At 29.1 ft/s, Duran ranks in the 92nd percentile in sprint speed, and the projection has him at 22 stolen bases, which tracks cleanly. The trouble is everything happening at the plate: a 34.4% whiff rate and a 34.7% chase rate leave him with a .293 xwOBA, and the projection consequence is a .212/.273/.364 line across 630 PA that reads like a fast man who can't get on base reliably enough to weaponize his speed. The 10.2% barrel rate is legitimately above average, so if the contact quality ever pairs with real zone discipline, you get a different player; if the swing decisions don't improve, you're looking at a high-SB outfielder with a .637 OPS and a roster question attached to him.

reports.name: Wei-En Lin
reports.published_report: The WHIP is 1.0 across AAA & AA, and that's the most honest thing in this profile. Wei-En Lin is limiting baserunners at an elite clip for a 20-year-old, and his 17 walks in 53 innings translate to a 3.2 BB/9 at the MLB level, matching what an average big-league starter allows, which means the command is functional but not a separator. The strikeouts are the catch: 54 punchouts across AAA & AA sounds fine until the MLB translation comes back at 8.0 K/9, a tick below where the average MLB pitcher lands, and the whole profile hinges on whether he can generate more whiffs against better hitters than he's seeing now. If the contact management holds and the swing-and-miss ticks up, he becomes a multi-inning reliever with a useful K-BB%; if neither develops, you've got a depth arm who keeps the ball off the bases until the wrong hitter comes along.

reports.name: Garrett Mitchell
reports.published_report: The contact is the problem, and the exit velocity makes it agonizing. Mitchell runs a 92.6 mph average exit velocity with a 13.8% barrel rate, both well into the top quarter of the league, but a 36.7% whiff rate erases a significant portion of what that quality of contact would otherwise earn. His 22.8% chase rate is genuinely disciplined, which means the whiff damage is happening inside the zone rather than from expanding it, and at 31.7% K% that's a hard ceiling on a profile that has the raw tools to be a plus regular. If the whiff rate ever comes down even modestly, the 11.7% walk rate plus a 98th-percentile sprint speed plus that exit velocity stack into something considerably more valuable than .774 OPS, a well-above-average outfielder rather than what he is now; if it doesn't, he's a useful but limited piece with a frustrating amount of untapped power sitting underneath.

reports.name: Heriberto Hernández
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power translation is genuinely odd here: a 51.4% hard-hit rate and 92.2 mph average exit velocity, yet a 33.6% whiff rate that sits near the bottom of the league. The raw hitting quality is legitimate, the swing-and-miss problem is just as real, and those two facts point in opposite directions. When he connects, he does damage, a .497 xSLG and 13.0% barrel rate say so, but 26.5% strikeouts drag the projection toward .238/.310/.457 over 428 plate appearances rather than anything more comfortable. If the whiff rate comes down even a tick, there's a 25-homer, above-average OPS outfielder in there. If it doesn't, he's a platoon-friendly power bat whose strikeouts keep him from holding a full-time role.

If a swing-and-miss pitch develops, the command floor makes him worth tracking; if it doesn't, he's a depth arm whose contact profile will find him out at the highest level.

reports.name: Jim Jarvis
reports.published_report:
The contact-first shortstop profile is the whole argument here, and the power is what keeps the ceiling in check. Jim Jarvis is hitting .313 at AAA with 46 walks against 55 strikeouts in 348 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 18.9% in a league that runs 22.0%, his walk rate at 10.8% where the field sits at 8.5%. The 32 stolen bases are loud. But six home runs and a .148 ISO at AAA translate to .13 against MLB pitching, and nothing in the shape of this profile suggests that gap narrows.

If the bat-to-ball and speed carry over, he's a low-end everyday shortstop; if a big league defense solves him, he's a reserve.

If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.
